candidates.label: Pragmatism — pragmatic-maxim criterion
candidates.scope: A scoped comparison of the pragmatic method for clarifying disputed ideas, not a complete pragmatist worldview.

existingAffinity.name: Pragmatism
existingAffinity.context: Classical pragmatism begins with Peirce, James, and Dewey; later pragmatists disagree about truth and realism. This entry compares the shared method of clarifying ideas through conceivable consequences, not a complete pragmatist worldview.
discriminators: Revisability alone does not establish the pragmatic maxim.
Practical bearings clarify meaning; they do not make convenience the sole truth condition.
Treating practical consequences as one helpful clue does not settle the empty-dispute criterion.
nonEntailments: Pragmatism does not entail that a useful belief is automatically true.
It does not entail atheism or rejection of mind-independent reality.
Agreement with this method does not establish the whole pragmatist tradition.

criteria.doctrine: Disputed ideas should be clarified through their conceivable effects on experience or conduct; if two formulations have no conceivable difference in those effects, their apparent conceptual difference is not substantive.
Inquiry can yield knowledge while remaining open to correction.
Inquiry is an ongoing practice of testing and revising claims.
Classical and later pragmatists disagree about realism and how to understand truth.

nonEntailments: a single pragmatist theory of truth
limitations: Classical and later pragmatists disagree about truth and realism.
Only the pragmatic-maxim criterion is treated as defining in this scoped profile.

candidates.label: Experience-grounded knowledge of the external world — scoped criterion
candidates.scope: Whether claims about concrete external reality require experiential evidence; not a complete account of empiricism or concept acquisition.

existingAffinity.name: Experience grounded external-world knowledge
existingAffinity.context: A subject-scoped empiricist comparison about factual knowledge of the concrete external world. It is not a claim that all knowledge, concepts, mathematics, or moral truths arise from the senses.
neighbors: a priori rationalism about external facts
discriminators: Trust in science does not establish that experience is the ultimate source of external-world knowledge.

nonEntailments: This position does not entail atheism, physicalism, or that mathematics has no a priori warrant.
It does not entail that observation alone is sufficient without reasoning or that every historical empiricist holds the same view.

criteria.doctrine: Knowledge claims about concrete external reality ultimately require experiential evidence; reasoning alone cannot establish new external-world facts.
Experience is the ultimate source of concepts used to describe the external world.
Empiricists differ about how far experience constrains mathematics, morality, and other domains.

limitations: The instrument's proposition is restricted to factual claims about ordinary external reality.
No current route directly tests the origin of all concepts or the status of mathematics and morality.

candidates.label: Ethical Egoism — universal self-priority and maximization distinction
candidates.scope: Separates the normative claim that each agent ought to prioritize their own good from the stronger criterion that rightness is maximization of the agent's good.

existingAffinity.name: Ethical egoism
existingAffinity.context: A normative thesis about what is morally right for each agent, distinct from psychological claims about what people in fact want and from Stirnerian ownness. The pilot cannot settle the full if-and-only-if account of rightness.
discriminators: Permission to pursue personal projects is weaker than a universal moral prescription to prioritize self-interest.
Stirnerian ownness can reject the fixed self-interest duty that ethical egoism asserts.
nonEntailments: Ethical egoism does not entail that everyone is in fact selfish.
It does not entail exploitative conduct or Rand's life-grounded moral theory.
Denying an independent need-based moral reason does not imply indifference, refusal to help, or inability to cooperate for self-interested reasons.

criteria.doctrine: Each person morally ought to make their own long-term good the ultimate end of their actions; another person’s need alone supplies no independent moral reason.
An act is morally right if and only if it best advances the agent's own good, rather than merely permitting self-regard.
The theory needs some account of what counts as an agent's good.
Whether the self-interest thesis is also a requirement of rationality is a distinct question.

blockingCoreGaps.proposition: An act is morally right if and only if it best advances the agent's own good.

limitations: The active direct proposition addresses exclusive moral self-priority, not a complete maximizing rightness criterion.

existingItemLeads.itemText: When two formulations have no conceivable difference in their consequences, that is a reason to question whether their disagreement is substantive.
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether a conceptual disagreement with no conceivable consequence is substantive.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: This unadministered candidate directly approaches the pragmatic maxim and could be reviewed as an additional evidence unit or route discriminator. It does not currently contribute to the public rule; EPI103 and EPI123 form the governed Full-route path.

existingItemLeads.itemText: The meaning of a philosophical distinction can always be settled without considering any possible consequence for experience or conduct.
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether meaning can always be settled without considering possible consequences for experience or conduct.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: This unadministered candidate is an overbroad reverse-key statement: the pragmatic maxim does not imply that every philosophical distinction is settled by experiential consequences. It should not be used as an opposition pole without semantic review.

existingItemLeads.itemText: What a person ultimately has most reason to do is whatever best promotes that person’s own long-term good.
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether an agent's own long-term good supplies the ultimate practical reason.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: NEI103–NEI105 target rational egoism about practical reasons. They are not in public routes and cannot establish whether moral rightness requires maximizing the agent's own good.

existingItemLeads.itemText: A stranger faces serious harm. You could prevent it at modest cost to yourself. Assume helping would not advance your own long-term good. What moral weight does the stranger's need have?
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether another person's need supplies an independent moral reason when helping does not advance one's own good.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: This scenario is already used by construct-NE15 on Full and can help assess exclusive moral self-priority. It does not test whether rightness is constituted by maximizing the agent's own good.

existingItemLeads.itemText: Respecting established roles and authorities can have moral value apart from the immediate consequences.
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether inherited roles or authority can have moral value apart from immediate consequences.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: This broad candidate wording does not distinguish ritual cultivation, reciprocal role duties, or Confucian role ethics. It is not administered on a public route.

existingItemLeads.itemText: When judging someone's conduct, how relevant is whether they violated a legitimate duty attached to their role or position?
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether violation of a legitimate role-attached duty matters morally.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: MFI017 and MFI027 feed the public moral-concern-authority proposition on all routes. This supports a general role-duty criterion, but not Confucian-specific reciprocal roles, ritual, or ethical cultivation.

existingItemLeads.itemText: A person openly violates a legitimate duty attached to an accepted role, but no immediate harm results. How morally relevant is the breach of duty?
existingItemLeads.distinction: Whether breaching an accepted role duty matters when no immediate harm results.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: MFI027 is paired with MFI017 under the public moral-concern-authority rule on all routes. It does not identify Confucian ritual or establish a general Confucian doctrine of role ethics.

existingItemLeads.itemText: Keeping customs handed down by my family, culture, or religion.
existingItemLeads.distinction: Priority assigned to maintaining inherited customs.
existingItemLeads.conclusion: The Full route uses this as a value-priority response. It does not measure ritual as ethical cultivation or role-specific moral duties.

futureDiscriminatorNeeds.distinction: Moral rightness as maximizing the agent's own good versus universal self-priority without a maximizing rightness criterion.
futureDiscriminatorNeeds.reason: NEI121 on Full tests whether another's need gives an independent moral reason; NEI103–NEI105 concern practical reasons. Neither directly asks whether rightness is constituted by maximizing the agent's own good.

futureDiscriminatorNeeds.distinction: The justification and psychological basis of inductive inference.
futureDiscriminatorNeeds.reason: No active or reviewed candidate public item isolates Hume's problem of induction from generic evidence, fallibilism, or external-world warrant. Existing temporal and causal items address different distinctions.

futureDiscriminatorNeeds.distinction: Ritual as ethical cultivation and reciprocal responsibilities tied to social roles.
futureDiscriminatorNeeds.reason: MFI017/MFI027 measure generic moral relevance of role-attached duties and SOI003/SOI027 measure relational aspects of identity. These are useful partial evidence, not Confucian ritual, reciprocity, or cultivation; MFI005 and VAI027 do not close that gap.

futureDiscriminatorNeeds.distinction: Virtue as the only genuine good and the status of preferred indifferents.
futureDiscriminatorNeeds.reason: The active character-counts proposition and ME09 human-life grounding do not establish virtue as the only good; candidate MFI004 concerns group loyalty as a virtue, not the Stoic value thesis.

futureDiscriminatorNeeds.distinction: Rand's specific account of rational egoism, rights, and political authority.
futureDiscriminatorNeeds.reason: Existing life-grounding, self-priority, market, and generic rights propositions do not establish Objectivism's integrated ethical and political derivation.
